title: 5 Things UXers Need to Stop Doing
intro: A one-page index to Calabro's recurring arguments — five habits that keep producing bad UX.

topics.title: 5 Things UXers Need to Stop Doing

learn.title: Two kinds of weaponising
learn.text:
**Jakob's Law.** One popular app isn't a convention. Compare across a set of similar products before claiming users already know a pattern.

**“Conversational UX”.** It's about how an interaction unfolds, not casual wording — and casual wording can disguise interruptions, shaming or upsells. Test whether the language helps the task.

try.q: A microcopy rewrite makes an upsell sound friendly. Is that conversational UX?
options: No — it's casual wording over an interruption
Yes, if the tone matches the brand voice
Yes, if users rate the copy positively
Only if the upsell can be dismissed easily
try.explain: Conversational UX is about how the interaction unfolds, not how chatty it sounds.

learn.title: Two kinds of throwing away evidence
learn.text:
**Time-on-task data.** Don't discard it because the sample is small or the numbers look messy. Lead with the median, report the range and individual cases, and explain the slow ones.

**Institutional knowledge used to shut down work.** Best practice is the default; whoever wants the exception carries the burden of proof.

try.q: Someone says “our users are different” to stop a usability recommendation. Who carries the burden of proof?
options: The person claiming the exception
The researcher making the recommendation
Whoever has worked here longest
The product manager who owns the area
try.explain: Best practice is the default position.

right.label: What to do instead
items: Median, range, and the slow cases

learn.title: Style guides that only describe looks
learn.text:
Document **states and behaviour**, not just colour and spacing.

Otherwise developers end up making the UX decisions — at build time, without the context.

try.q: A style guide specifies a button's colour and padding but not its disabled or loading behaviour. What happens?
options: Developers decide the behaviour at build time
The button renders inconsistently across browsers
Designers have to review every pull request
The component fails accessibility testing automatically
try.explain: Undocumented behaviour becomes someone else's decision.

options: Indexes five arguments Calabro makes elsewhere
Introduces five new research methods
Lists the five most common usability errors
Ranks UX practices by business impact
test.explain: It is a one-page summary pointing at the longer pieces.

test.q: What should you lead with when reporting time on task?
options: The median
The mean
The fastest completion
The number of participants
test.explain: Then the range, the individual cases, and an explanation of the slow ones.

test.q: Why is one popular app not enough to claim a convention?
options: A convention needs prevalence across similar products
Popular apps change their patterns too often
Users rarely use more than one app in a category
The app may be under a different design licence
test.explain: Compare across a set of similar products.

test.q: Which habit is on the list?
options: Using institutional knowledge to end a discussion
Running too many usability tests per quarter
Writing research plans that are too detailed
Reporting confidence intervals to stakeholders
test.explain: The other three are things he recommends doing.

test.q: What is the risk of a looks-only style guide?
options: UX decisions get made in code
Designers copy components inconsistently
Brand colours drift between products
New hires take longer to onboard
test.explain: States and behaviour belong in the guide.
